newsitem.title: UK: Britain ready to evacuate volcano islanders.
newsitem.headline: Britain ready to evacuate volcano islanders.

text.p: A British warship was on Monday standing by to evacuate residents from the Carribbean island of Montserrat as fears grew of a massive volcanic eruption there.
Britain said the island's volcano had become more dangerous and a voluntary partial evacuation of the 4,000 to 5,000 remaining residents was being organised.

Officials from the Foreign Office and the Overseas Development Office were holding talks on the worsening situation and British warship H.M.S. Liverpool was ready to take anyone who wanted to leave the British colony.
"With all the smoke and ash from the volcano, it's impossible to fly," a Foreign Office spokesman said.

He said a ferry service to neighbouring islands such as Antigua and Guadeloupe was another option for those wishing to leave Montserrat, which is in the Leeward Islands chain at the northeastern end of the Caribbean.

Montserrat's volcano, in the Soufriere Hills not far from the capital, Plymouth, started spewing ash and rock in July 1995, having been dormant for some 400 years. But the situation took a turn for the worse over the weekend.
Britain's International Development Minister George Foulkes said earlier that the possibility of a "massive, cataclysmic-intensive eruption" of the volcano could no longer be ruled out.
"Over the past 24 hours the volcano has become much more dangerous. As a result we have agreed to this voluntary partial evacuation of anyone who wants to leave in the wake of this information."

Foulkes said experts at the Montserrat Volcano Observatory had warned him the consequences of such an event, if it did occur, would be extreme and anywhere on the island could be significantly threatened. Talks were under way with the island's governor, Frank Savage.
The evacuation plan would take effect immediately and people would be given the opportunity to leave at once, he added.

The island's population is down to less than half the 11,000 living there before the volcano became active again but most of them are now in the north, the opposite end of the island from the volcano.

On Saturday, scientific advice prompted the authorities to order the evacuation of the central area of the island, where some people had fled after Plymouth was hit by a series of eruptions two weeks ago.
Islanders will be given the choice of both if and where they want to go.

"Not everyone wants to go to the UK. Some have gone to the U.S. where there is a big Montserrat community and others may want to go to neighbouring islands on a temporary basis," the Foreign Office spokesman said.
